report.headline: Projected to be a low-usage role player in the NBA, with usage rate falling from 15.5% to 11.9% and a true-shooting projection that the model cannot be trusted to make

projection.text: Player A's usage rate is projected to fall to 11.9% in the NBA, down from 15.5% in the G League and well below the target season's league-average usage rate of 20.1%; the 80% interval (6.4%-17.4%) spans roughly two standard deviations of the league's usage distribution (5.5%), so the model can place him relative to peers but cannot pin down an individual number.

risks.text: Usage rate projects to drop sharply, from 15.5% in the G League to 11.9% in the NBA, roughly 1.5 standard deviations below the target season's league-average usage rate of 20.1%, signaling a diminished offensive role.
The 95% interval for usage rate (3.5%-20.3%) covers nearly the full spread of NBA usage rates, reflecting substantial individual-level uncertainty even though the model can rank players in aggregate.

The true-shooting projection of 56.4% is unreliable because the model does no better than a naive league-mean baseline on this metric (MAE 4.7% vs 4.7%), so it should not be used to judge his likely NBA efficiency.

The estimate rests on a modest historical sample of 45 GL->NBA transitions, and two full seasons elapsed between the source season and the move, both of which add to the uncertainty of applying the model to this case.

strengths.text: In the G League, Player A posted a true shooting percentage of 61.0%, one full standard deviation above the league average, indicating clear scoring efficiency.
Nearly two-thirds of his shot attempts (65.9%) came from three-point range, paired with a low turnover rate of 7.0%, consistent with a low-usage, high-value floor-spacing profile.

Historically, efficiency metrics carry over from the G League to the NBA more than usage does: the fitted slope for true shooting is 0.801 versus 0.531 for usage, suggesting his shooting skill is more likely to persist than his shot volume.

uncertainty.text: The model's estimates are fitted on players who, on average, sat +0.27 SD above their own league before moving; Player A, at -0.97 SD in G League usage, sits well below that typical mover profile, which adds to the uncertainty here. The usage-rate model modestly beats a trivial league-mean baseline (MAE 3.3% vs 4.3%), so that projection carries some signal, but the true-shooting model performs no better than simply guessing the league mean (MAE 4.7% vs 4.7%), so the projected true-shooting percentage of 56.4% should not be treated as informative.
